query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX alloys, when X is Si or Al, the preferential oxidation of these elements at high temperatures leads to the formation of a continuous, coherent inner oxide layer (SiO2 or Al2O3) that is chemically inert and slow growing, thereby resisting cracking or spallation. In contrast, when X is Mn, the resulting oxide is a more non-uniform, mixed-phase oxide with greater thermal expansion mismatch that tends to crack under prolonged exposure above 900 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys processed into a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with a homogenized microstructure.
generation.intervention: Varying the X element among Si, Al, and Mn in otherwise composition-matched CrFeCoNiX alloys to isolate the effect of the reactive element on oxide scale formation.
generation.conditions: Oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 925–950 °C), with exposure durations on the order of 100 hours or longer. Testing may include controlled lab environments with defined oxygen partial pressures or simulated corrosive gas mixtures.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and coherency of the initially formed oxide scale at the alloy surface, especially the formation of a continuous, slow-growing layer (i.e. SiO2 or Al2O3) that adheres well to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the high oxygen affinity of Si and Al drives their preferential oxidation. The resulting oxide layers (SiO2 or Al2O3) are dense, have low ionic diffusivity, and a lower thermal expansion mismatch with the underlying alloy, resulting in a protective barrier that grows slowly and maintains integrity. Conversely, Mn oxidizes into mixed-valence oxides that form a less coherent, more stressed barrier prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Si or Al will form a stable, coherent, and slow-growing protective oxide layer that maintains integrity under high-temperature oxidation, whereas alloys with Mn will develop unstable and spallation-prone oxide scales.
generation.baseline: The comparison is made against the Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX alloy under identical processing and testing conditions, which is expected to form a non-protective, cracked oxide scale.
generation.boundary: Findings are valid within the regime of high-temperature oxidation (>900 °C) in environments where oxidative or corrosive conditions prevail and for compositions maintained in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state. Deviations in processing parameters or microstructural states may influence oxide behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While the oxidation kinetics and stress-mismatch considerations support the mechanism, variations in alloy microstructure (single- vs multiphase) and local chemical homogeneity may introduce uncertainties in the precise performance of the oxide scales. Detailed phase characterization and stress analysis of the oxide/substrate interface are needed to fully validate the mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys with X = Si, Al, and Mn by identical melting and homogenization processes to ensure a comparably uniform single- or multiphase solid solution. Expose samples to an oxidative environment (e.g., air or a defined oxygen-rich gas mixture) at temperatures above 900 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, perform surface and cross-sectional microscopy (SEM/TEM), X-ray diffraction, and thermal-mechanical analyses to assess oxide scale morphology, thickness, phase composition, coherence, and presence of cracks or spallation.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate
Crystal structure and phase identification of the oxide scale
Interfacial adhesion and evidence of cracking/spallation
Residual stress measurements within the oxide film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with Si or Al do not exhibit a significantly more continuous, coherent, and slow-growing oxide layer compared to the Mn-containing alloy (i.e. if no observable difference in oxide integrity and spallation behavior is found between the different X elements), then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.
